vignette:
It was a Thursday evening in late October when the men came. Marcus had been in the regional office in Mogadishu for only three weeks, part of a financial oversight team auditing humanitarian contracts. The armed men who took him from his guesthouse did not speak to him for the first six hours. They kept him in a windowless room with a concrete floor, and for seventeen days they moved him between three different locations, always at night, always with a cloth bag over his head. The smells from that room—diesel fumes, sweat, the metallic tang of old blood on a rag they used to gag him—were the first things that came back to him now, unbidden and overwhelming, more real than anything in his present life. The memory of that room felt clearer and more detailed than his memory of his own apartment in Chicago.

When he finally returned home, Marcus tried to resume his work as a financial analyst. But the open-plan office, with its sudden silences when a colleague paused mid-sentence, became unbearable. A hush falling over a conference room would send his pulse racing before he had time to register why. What frightened him most was the feeling that his body was reacting to a threat that his mind could not see. He had come to believe that he was no longer the same person who had gone to Mogadishu. During his captivity, he had signed documents under duress, documents that implicated local contractors in fraud he knew nothing about. The memory of that pen moving across the paper made him feel hollow, as though he had become an object that others could use—he had acted in ways that went against who he was, and the men who had forced him faced no consequences. They were still out there. The silence of the office, the cries of a child in the grocery store, even a colleague’s hand on his shoulder in greeting—each of these moments brought the smell of the bag back into his nostrils, and with it the understanding that he had been reduced to something less than a person.

Months passed, and Marcus found himself sleeping poorly. He had difficulty falling asleep because a part of him needed to stay alert, listening for footsteps or the click of a lock. The hypervigilance followed him into every room of his own home; he felt on guard even inside his apartment, checking the locks three times before bed and scanning the street below before drawing the curtains. He would sometimes catch himself smelling diesel in the middle of the night, and the memory would arrive with such force that the bedroom walls seemed to dissolve, leaving him back on the concrete floor. These intrusions made him feel more like an object—a thing that could be moved and silenced—and less like a person with choices. The cycle tightened. Every time he felt alert, the memories felt closer, and every time the memories came, the sense of being a hollow object deepened, and that feeling made him scan the room for threats again.

He divorced eight months after returning. His wife had tried to hold him, and he had frozen. Physical affection, even a hug goodnight, now made him feel trapped. When she cried, he could not stay in the room. The sound of a child crying in the supermarket would send him to the car, his hands shaking. He had come to believe that the people responsible had gotten away with what they did, and that knowledge sat inside him like a stone. He stopped going to the office. He worked from home, where he could control the silence. But the silence itself became a trigger—the sudden quiet of his own apartment when a video call ended, the absence of sound in the hallway—and he would find himself standing at the window, watching the street, alert and waiting, with the smell of diesel in his throat and the memory of a pen signing his name to something false, and the thought that he had become a thing that could be used, and that no one had answered for it.

He came to the clinic because his supervisor had told him he would lose his job if he did not return to the office. Marcus was afraid of the office. But he was also afraid that if he stayed in his apartment much longer, the silence would swallow him.
